evals.prompt: Stakeholders keep finding bad numbers in our dashboards — null customer IDs, duplicated orders, and data that's a day stale. We're on dbt + Snowflake. Set up data quality checks.
evals.expected_output: Maps each symptom to a concrete check (not_null/unique dbt tests, source freshness), places checks at the ingestion boundary first and critical marts second, assigns severity (error blocks, warn alerts), routes failures to an owner, and uses lineage to scope which downstream models and dashboards a failure affects
assertions: Maps each reported symptom to a concrete check: not_null/unique dbt tests for the IDs and duplicates, and source freshness checks for the staleness
Places checks at the right layers: the source/ingestion boundary first, then critical marts — not only on the final dashboards
Assigns severity levels (error vs warn) and defines what blocks the pipeline versus what only alerts
Sets up alerting and ownership so failures reach someone who acts, instead of failing silently
Uses lineage to scope blast radius — which downstream models or dashboards a failing check affects

evals.prompt: An upstream team owns the events we ingest and keeps renaming columns and changing types without telling us. Our pipeline breaks silently every few weeks. What should we put in place?
evals.expected_output: Proposes a producer/consumer data contract (schema, types, semantics, SLA) enforced at the ingestion boundary so violations fail loudly at entry; shifts validation left into the producer's CI or publish path; adds versioning/deprecation windows for breaking changes; and backstops enforcement with schema-drift and volume/distribution anomaly detection
assertions: Proposes an explicit data contract between producer and consumer (schema, types, semantics, SLAs), not just more downstream tests
Enforces the schema at the ingestion boundary so violations fail loudly at entry instead of propagating silently
Shifts checks left: contract validation in the producer's CI or at publish time
Covers change management for breaking changes: contract versioning or a deprecation window
Adds detection for what enforcement misses: schema-drift alerts or anomaly checks on volume/distributions

evals.prompt: A customer told us our revenue dashboard had been wrong for three days before anyone here noticed. The upstream team had renamed a column. I need to make sure that never happens silently again.
evals.expected_output: 'Never happens silently' is two problems the roster does not separate. Knowing the data is wrong — a schema-drift check and a freshness check that would have caught a renamed column on the first run, plus a contract with the upstream team so the rename surfaces before it lands — is this skill's work, delivered concretely. Getting a person's attention once something is known to be wrong, including who is paged and on what threshold, is observability-design's. A good answer treats detection and notification as separate failures, because this incident failed at both.
assertions: Separates the two halves: detecting that the data is wrong, versus getting a person's attention when it is
Refers to observability-design for alert routing and who gets paged
Delivers the detection half itself — a schema-drift or freshness check that would have caught the renamed column — rather than deferring the whole request
Raises a contract with the upstream team so the rename surfaces before it lands, not only afterwards
